aliases.value: barred dove (older name per Bishop Museum)

resources.title: Himalayan snowcock
resources.description: Identify the himalayan snowcock (Tetraogallus himalayensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Himalayan snowcock (Tetraogallus himalayensis): Very large: 64-74 cm, 2-3.5 kg, wingspan 1.1-1.3 m. Chestnut stripes around a pale face and throat. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: In the US, NatureServe records the species in Nevada (introduced); Audubon calls its U.S. range limited.

rangeSummary.value: In the US, NatureServe records the species in Nevada (introduced); Audubon calls its U.S. range limited.

identification.text: Very large: 64-74 cm, 2-3.5 kg, wingspan 1.1-1.3 m.
Chestnut stripes around a pale face and throat.
Sexes similar, male slightly larger.

behavior.text: Displaying male gives a loud fluting whistle, plus chuckling clucks
Feeds on roots, tubers and seeds
Nest is a ground scrape, often sheltered by rocks or grass clumps; 4-6 eggs

resources.title: Plain chachalaca
resources.description: Identify the plain chachalaca (Ortalis vetula), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Plain chachalaca (Ortalis vetula): Large, long-tailed, small-headed; 50-66 cm, 680 g-1.1 kg. Dull olive brown, greyer head, buff belly; may show red on the throat. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Extreme southern Texas (Rio Grande Valley) south through Mexico and Central America; NatureServe also records it in Georgia.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes some authors consider it conspecific with O. leucogaster.

rangeSummary.value: Extreme southern Texas (Rio Grande Valley) south through Mexico and Central America; NatureServe also records it in Georgia.

identification.text: Large, long-tailed, small-headed; 50-66 cm, 680 g-1.1 kg.
Dull olive brown, greyer head, buff belly; may show red on the throat.
Wide black tail feathers with white tips; sexes similar.

habitat.text: Subtropical woods, river groves and dense brush, usually near water in south Texas; native ebony, hackberry, huisache and mesquite woodland and overgrown orchard edges.

behavior.text: Loud, raucous 'cha-cha-lac', often in chorus at dawn and dusk; male's voice lower than female's
Forages on the ground or in shrubs and trees, climbing about in thin branches
Mostly vegetarian: berries (coyotillo, pigeonberry, hackberry), seeds, leaves, buds, flowers; a few insects and snails
Nest is a stick platform 4-15 ft up in dense cover

resources.title: Kalij pheasant
resources.description: Identify the kalij pheasant (Lophura leucomelanos), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Kalij pheasant (Lophura leucomelanos): About 33 in (84 cm) long; males black with a grey belly, females mottled brown. Bare red skin patch around the eyes and a crest of feathers atop the head. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to southern Asia; first brought to Hawaii in 1962 as a gamebird. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: formerly L. leucomelana; Sibley and Monroe (1990) argued the original spelling leucomelana is correct.

rangeSummary.value: Native to southern Asia; first brought to Hawaii in 1962 as a gamebird. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

identification.text: About 33 in (84 cm) long; males black with a grey belly, females mottled brown.
Bare red skin patch around the eyes and a crest of feathers atop the head.

habitat.text: Upland areas (Hawaii).

behavior.text: Relatively common in upland areas; often seen scurrying by

resources.title: Green pheasant
resources.description: Identify the green pheasant (Phasianus versicolor), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Green pheasant (Phasianus versicolor): Male: dark green breast, neck, mantle and flanks, bluish-purplish hood with ear tufts, red wattles, long pale grey-banded tail. Female: smaller than male, shorter tail, brownish-black with dark brown feathers fringed pale brown. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and smaller Japanese islands; introduced populations in Hawaii are reported stable; introduction to mainland North America was unsuccessful, and it has been crossed with common pheasants on some North American game farms.

taxonomicNotes.text: Wikipedia notes some authorities treat it as a subspecies of Phasianus colchicus; Bishop Museum's Hawaii monograph files the Hawaii 'Green Pheasant' as Phasianus colchicus versicolor.
Treated as a species by Hawaii's rules and most checklists; some authorities fold it into the common pheasant

rangeSummary.value: Native to Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and smaller Japanese islands; introduced populations in Hawaii are reported stable; introduction to mainland North America was unsuccessful, and it has been crossed with common pheasants on some North American game farms.

identification.text: Male: dark green breast, neck, mantle and flanks, bluish-purplish hood with ear tufts, red wattles, long pale grey-banded tail.
Female: smaller than male, shorter tail, brownish-black with dark brown feathers fringed pale brown.

Compared with the ring-necked pheasant: Considered by some authorities the same species; Hawaii records also mention a melanistic 'mutant' or blue form of ring-necked pheasant that can resemble green pheasant.

habitat.text: Woodland and forest edges, brush, grassland and parkland.

behavior.text: Omnivorous: worms, insects, grains and plants
Breeds March-June, 6-15 eggs incubated 23-25 days

resources.title: Japanese quail
resources.description: Identify the japanese quail (Coturnix japonica), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Japanese quail (Coturnix japonica): Dark brown with buff mottling above, lighter brown below; whitish stripe above the eye. Males usually show rufous on the breast and black flecking on the throat; females usually lack these. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to East Asia; domesticated since about the 13th century. NatureServe records it in Hawaii; Hawaii DLNR lists it among Hawaii's game birds.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: sometimes regarded as conspecific with C. coturnix, but the two are sympatric in Mongolia; ADW also keeps them separate.

rangeSummary.value: Native to East Asia; domesticated since about the 13th century. NatureServe records it in Hawaii; Hawaii DLNR lists it among Hawaii's game birds.

identification.text: Dark brown with buff mottling above, lighter brown below; whitish stripe above the eye.
Males usually show rufous on the breast and black flecking on the throat; females usually lack these.
Legs and bill orangish to pinkish grey; wild birds about 90-115 g; wing 92-101 mm.
Compared with the common quail: Very similar; the two are sympatric in Mongolia without interbreeding (ADW, NatureServe).

behavior.text: Male call is typically three notes ('deep hollow sounds' repeated); seven distinct male displays and calls recorded in captive birds
Migratory: breeds in northern Japan, Korea and Russia, winters in southeast China, Hainan, Taiwan and southern Japan
Eats grass seeds plus small worms, insect larvae and other invertebrates, especially in summer

resources.title: Gray francolin
resources.description: Identify the gray francolin (Ortygornis pondicerianus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gray francolin (Ortygornis pondicerianus): About a foot long, distinct rows of brown feathers with a pale face and throat. Sexes look similar; males may be slightly larger. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to India; introduced to Hawaii. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: formerly (AOU 1983, 1998) placed in Francolinus; genetic data indicate Francolinus is not monophyletic. ADW still files it as Francolinus pondicerianus.

rangeSummary.value: Native to India; introduced to Hawaii. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

identification.text: About a foot long, distinct rows of brown feathers with a pale face and throat.
Sexes look similar; males may be slightly larger.

habitat.text: Dry areas.

behavior.text: Loud call often heard in the morning
Common in dry areas; easily seen near lawns and roads at dawn and dusk (Hawaii)

resources.title: Black francolin
resources.description: Identify the black francolin (Francolinus francolinus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Black francolin (Francolinus francolinus): Male: black head and chest with white face patch and belly spots, reddish collar, brown back. Female: mottled brown with a hint of reddish collar. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to India; introduced to Hawaii in 1959. NatureServe records it in Florida.

rangeSummary.value: Native to India; introduced to Hawaii in 1959. NatureServe records it in Florida.

identification.text: Male: black head and chest with white face patch and belly spots, reddish collar, brown back.
Female: mottled brown with a hint of reddish collar.

habitat.text: Thick vegetation, brushy areas and tall grassland, generally near water; mosaic of forest and cultivated land, not interior forest.

behavior.text: Loud creaking call during breeding season
Scares easily and hides, preferring to run rather than flush (Hawaii)

resources.title: Erckel's spurfowl
resources.description: Identify the erckel's spurfowl (Pternistis erckelii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Erckel's spurfowl (Pternistis erckelii): About 16 in (40 cm), brown with white streaky spots. Chestnut feathers on top of the head and a white throat. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to Ethiopia and Sudan; introduced to Hawaii in 1957. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe primary name is Erckel's Francolin; formerly placed in Francolinus (AOU 1983, 1998), transferred to Pternistis by AOS (2019). ADW and DLNR still use Francolinus / Erckel's Francolin.
Hawaii rules call it Erckel's francolin

rangeSummary.value: Native to Ethiopia and Sudan; introduced to Hawaii in 1957. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

identification.text: About 16 in (40 cm), brown with white streaky spots.
Chestnut feathers on top of the head and a white throat.

habitat.text: Upland dry grasslands (Hawaii).

behavior.text: Scares easily and hides, preferring to run rather than flush
Loud laughing cackle, especially in the morning

resources.title: Chestnut-bellied sandgrouse
resources.description: Identify the chestnut-bellied sandgrouse (Pterocles exustus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Chestnut-bellied sandgrouse (Pterocles exustus). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Introduced to Hawaii Island by the Nevada game department as a trial for possible import to Nevada. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

taxonomicNotes.text: ADW places it in Charadriiformes, family Pteroclididae; NatureServe says the relationships of Pteroclididae are unclear (Charadriiformes vs Columbiformes; AOU 1998 incertae sedis). Order and family here follow ADW; not resolved. Field marks not sourced.

rangeSummary.value: Introduced to Hawaii Island by the Nevada game department as a trial for possible import to Nevada. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

behavior.text: Powerful flyer adapted to desert; on Hawaii Island flies mauka to makai to collect water
Carries water to the nest in absorbent breast feathers for young to drink

resources.title: Helmeted guineafowl
resources.description: Identify the helmeted guineafowl (Numida meleagris), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Helmeted guineafowl (Numida meleagris): Body feathers grey-black with white speckles; 51-64 cm, 1.1-1.8 kg; about 22 in in Hawaii. Bare head with sky-blue to dark-blue skin, a bony casque (larger in males) and wattles (smaller in females). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native across most of sub-Saharan Africa. In Hawaii, domestic-type birds have been released and live in open urban fields near ponds and wetlands.

rangeSummary.value: Native across most of sub-Saharan Africa. In Hawaii, domestic-type birds have been released and live in open urban fields near ponds and wetlands.

identification.text: Body feathers grey-black with white speckles; 51-64 cm, 1.1-1.8 kg; about 22 in in Hawaii.
Bare head with sky-blue to dark-blue skin, a bony casque (larger in males) and wattles (smaller in females).
Juveniles: less developed casque and wattles, paler face, grey-brown overall; chicks have longitudinal head stripes.

habitat.text: Exposed areas with some trees for roosting: grassland, savanna, cultivated land and scrub, often near water; avoids dense forest, desert and marsh.

behavior.text: Terrestrial flocks roost in trees at night; flocks of one pair up to 100 birds, largest in winter
Runs from danger and flies only as a last resort, steeply upward
Harsh dry calls carry far; male gives a single 'chek', female a two-note 'buck-wheat'
Omnivorous: seeds, grain, bulbs, roots, fruit, snails, beetles, ticks, small lizards; dust bathes daily

resources.title: Rock partridge
resources.description: Identify the rock partridge (Alectoris graeca), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Rock partridge (Alectoris graeca): Rotund; light brown back, grey breast, buff belly. White face with a sharply defined black gorget; rufous-streaked flanks; red legs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to southern Europe. The Wikipedia page says the name 'rock partridge' has been used in the US for several Alectoris species and hybrids, so North American records may not be this species.

taxonomicNotes.text: Wikipedia notes the English name 'rock partridge' is confused with stone partridge and misapplied to other Alectoris species and hybrids in the US.

rangeSummary.value: Native to southern Europe. The Wikipedia page says the name 'rock partridge' has been used in the US for several Alectoris species and hybrids, so North American records may not be this species.

identification.text: Rotund; light brown back, grey breast, buff belly.
White face with a sharply defined black gorget; rufous-streaked flanks; red legs.
Greyer on the back than a chukar and has a white, not yellowish, foreneck.
Compared with the chukar: Very similar; rock partridge is greyer on the back with a white foreneck instead of yellowish.
Compared with the red-legged partridge: Rock partridge's black gorget is sharply defined; red-legged has black streaking below the gorget.

habitat.text: Dry, open, often hilly country.

behavior.text: Prefers to run rather than fly when disturbed; short flight on rounded wings
Call: noisy 'ga-ga-ga-ga-chakera-chakera-chakera'
Takes a wide variety of seeds and some insects

resources.title: Red-legged partridge
resources.description: Identify the red-legged partridge (Alectoris rufa), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Red-legged partridge (Alectoris rufa): Sandy-brown above, pinkish-buff belly, pale grey breast. White face with a prominent gorget of black streaking, cream throat. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to France, Iberia and northwest Italy; naturalised in England and Wales. The page read does not describe North American populations.

rangeSummary.value: Native to France, Iberia and northwest Italy; naturalised in England and Wales. The page read does not describe North American populations.

identification.text: Sandy-brown above, pinkish-buff belly, pale grey breast.
White face with a prominent gorget of black streaking, cream throat.
Bold rufous-and-black flank bars (typically eight to ten), red bill and eye-ring, pinkish-red legs.
Compared with the rock partridge: Sharply defined black gorget without streaking below it; greyer back.

habitat.text: Dry lowlands such as farmland and open stony ground; ground nester.

behavior.text: Prefers running to flying; short flight on rounded wings
Call: three-syllable 'ka-chu-chu'
Seed eater; chicks rely on insects
Forms flocks outside the breeding season

resources.title: Spotted dove
resources.description: Identify the spotted dove (Spilopelia chinensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Spotted dove (Spilopelia chinensis): Mourning-dove size but bulkier, rounder tail, no black spots on the wings. Black collar with white spots is the best mark, less obvious on young birds (immatures lack the band). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to Asia; introduced from Asia to Hawaii in the 1800s and to California. NatureServe records it in California, Utah and Hawaii.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: the genus Streptopelia sensu lato is weakly supported as monophyletic; species placed in Spilopelia. ADW still files it as Streptopelia chinensis.

rangeSummary.value: Native to Asia; introduced from Asia to Hawaii in the 1800s and to California. NatureServe records it in California, Utah and Hawaii.

identification.text: Mourning-dove size but bulkier, rounder tail, no black spots on the wings.
Black collar with white spots is the best mark, less obvious on young birds (immatures lack the band).
Rosy breast, grey-brown plumage; 12-13 in.
Compared with the mourning dove: Spotted dove is bulkier with a rounder tail, has no black wing spots and shows the white-spotted black neck collar.

habitat.text: Residential areas, parks and river woods, mostly altered habitats: well-watered suburbs with trees and lawns, farms, stream groves including eucalyptus.

behavior.text: Calls a three-syllable rolling coo-coo-cooooo
Forages on the ground for seeds, in pairs or small groups; comes to feeders
Male display: steep climb with noisy wing-claps, then a gliding circle

resources.title: Zebra dove
resources.description: Identify the zebra dove (Geopelia striata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Zebra dove (Geopelia striata): Small, slender dove 20-23 cm with a long, narrow tail. Upperparts brownish-grey with black-and-white barring; underparts pinkish with black bars on the sides of the neck, breast and belly. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra and Java. Introduced to Hawaii in 1922 and now on all main islands, where it is one of the most abundant birds; established on other Pacific and Indian Ocean islands. Not established on the North American mainland in these sources.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the Australian Peaceful Dove (G. placida) and Wallacean Barred Dove (G. maugeus) may be conspecific with G. striata per Sibley and Monroe (1990); the Bishop Museum monograph notes most authors treat all three as separate species and treats Zebra Dove as monotypic.
Hawaii rules call it barred dove

rangeSummary.value: Native from southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra and Java. Introduced to Hawaii in 1922 and now on all main islands, where it is one of the most abundant birds; established on other Pacific and Indian Ocean islands. Not established on the North American mainland in these sources.

identification.text: Small, slender dove 20-23 cm with a long, narrow tail.
Upperparts brownish-grey with black-and-white barring; underparts pinkish with black bars on the sides of the neck, breast and belly.
Blue-grey face with bare blue skin around the eyes.
White tips to the tail feathers.
Juveniles duller and paler than adults.
Compared with the peaceful dove: Australian/New Guinea species that some authors have treated as part of the same species; not found in North America (NatureServe, Bishop Museum).
Compared with the barred dove: Lesser Sundas/Moluccas species sometimes lumped with Zebra Dove; not found in North America (Bishop Museum).

habitat.text: Scrub, farmland and open lowland country; common in parks and gardens. In Hawaii found mainly in dry lowlands, agricultural fields and suburban and urban areas, up to about 1000 m and occasionally 2300 m.

behavior.text: Forages alone or in pairs on bare ground, short grass or roads, scurrying with rodent-like movement
Eats small grass and weed seeds, plus insects and other small invertebrates
Call is a series of soft, staccato cooing notes
In Hawaii it can be quite tame around parks and outdoor eating areas, and flocks can gather at water holes in dry areas

resources.title: White-tipped dove
resources.description: Identify the white-tipped dove (Leptotila verreauxi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: White-tipped dove (Leptotila verreauxi): 25-30 cm, round-bodied and short-tailed with pale eyes. Lacks the black ear spot and black wing spots of Mourning Dove. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Permanent resident from northern Mexico and southern Texas (lower Rio Grande Valley) south to southern Brazil, Uruguay and eastern Argentina.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the Brazilian Dove (L. brasiliensis) is included in this species but regarded by some as a separate species (AOU 1983).

rangeSummary.value: Permanent resident from northern Mexico and southern Texas (lower Rio Grande Valley) south to southern Brazil, Uruguay and eastern Argentina.

identification.text: 25-30 cm, round-bodied and short-tailed with pale eyes.
Lacks the black ear spot and black wing spots of Mourning Dove.
Rich dark chestnut under the wings in flight.
Sexes similar.
Compared with the mourning dove: White-tipped is much rounder-bodied and shorter-tailed with pale eyes, and lacks the black ear spot and black wing spots.

habitat.text: Shady woodlands and river thickets; in southern Texas any dense low growth, most common in native woodland but also second growth. Elsewhere in its range mostly drier or more open woods; avoids unbroken rain forest.

behavior.text: Forages mostly on the ground, walking in woodland undergrowth; sometimes in low trees or shrubs
Usually solitary, not sociable like many doves; a few may gather at food sources
Eats seeds (grasses, mesquite, elm), berries and fruits such as hackberry and prickly pear, and possibly some insects
Song is a deep, drawn-out, descending coo lower pitched than most of our pigeons and doves

resources.title: Rock pigeon
resources.description: Identify the rock pigeon (Columba livia), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Rock pigeon (Columba livia): About 34 cm; ancestral (wild-type) plumage pale gray body with darker head, white rump and two black wing bars. Contrasty white underwings in flight. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to Eurasia; introduced and established throughout most of the world, including across North America.

rangeSummary.value: Native to Eurasia; introduced and established throughout most of the world, including across North America.

identification.text: About 34 cm; ancestral (wild-type) plumage pale gray body with darker head, white rump and two black wing bars.
Contrasty white underwings in flight.
Feral flocks include many other colour forms, some resembling native Band-tailed Pigeon.
Compared with the band-tailed pigeon: Wild native pigeon that some feral Rock Pigeon colour forms can suggest; Audubon gives no further separating marks.

habitat.text: Around cities, farms, cliffs and bridges; most common around cities and in suburbs and farms, occasionally in wild places far from human dwellings. In its native range nested on coastal and inland cliffs and gorges.

behavior.text: Forages mostly by walking on the ground, often in flocks
Eats mostly seeds; away from cities waste grain, grass and other seeds, sometimes berries or acorns; in cities largely food scraps
Not migratory; has good homing ability
Soft guttural cooing

resources.title: Mottled duck
resources.description: Identify the mottled duck (Anas fulvigula), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mottled duck (Anas fulvigula): Both sexes look like a darker version of a female Mallard. Bill bright yellow (male) or dull yellow (female). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Two natural resident ranges: the western Gulf Coast from Alabama west to Texas and south to Tamaulipas, and the Florida peninsula. Populations introduced from the 1970s exist in eastern Georgia and eastern South Carolina.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the species appears to constitute a superspecies with Mallard and American Black Duck and is sometimes included in Mallard (AOU 1983).

rangeSummary.value: Two natural resident ranges: the western Gulf Coast from Alabama west to Texas and south to Tamaulipas, and the Florida peninsula. Populations introduced from the 1970s exist in eastern Georgia and eastern South Carolina.

identification.text: Both sexes look like a darker version of a female Mallard.
Bill bright yellow (male) or dull yellow (female).
Blue wing patch (speculum) lacks the broad white borders of a Mallard.
Body paler and head more buff than American Black Duck.
Length about 50-58 cm.
Compared with the mallard (female): Mottled Duck is darker and its wing patch lacks Mallard's broad white borders.
Compared with the american black duck: Mottled Duck's body is paler and head more buff; Black Duck is rare in the deep south.
Compared with the mexican duck: Compare in the Southwest, from southern and western Texas to Arizona.

habitat.text: Marshes and open marshy country, wet prairies and rice fields; favors treeless country. In coastal areas usually fresh or brackish ponds adjacent to the coast rather than salt marsh.

behavior.text: Mostly non-migratory; makes local movements as habitat conditions change
Forages in shallow water, mostly dabbling at mud just below the surface, occasionally up-ending
Eats seeds of aquatic plants and grasses, insects, snails and occasionally small fish
Call is a loud quack like a Mallard's

resources.title: Mexican duck
resources.description: Identify the mexican duck (Anas diazi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mexican duck (Anas diazi): Both sexes resemble a female Mallard with mottled brown plumage but somewhat darker overall, especially on the tail and undertail. Blue wing patch (speculum) with white borders that may be narrower than a Mallard's. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico and west-central Texas south into the Mexican highlands. Non-breeding birds occur casually north through much of Colorado and Utah; accidental in California, Wyoming and Nebraska.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it was long treated as conspecific with Mallard (AOU 1983, 1998) and was newly separated as a species by AOS (2020) based on assortative mating and genomic data.
Split from mallard by the AOS in 2020

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico and west-central Texas south into the Mexican highlands. Non-breeding birds occur casually north through much of Colorado and Utah; accidental in California, Wyoming and Nebraska.

identification.text: Both sexes resemble a female Mallard with mottled brown plumage but somewhat darker overall, especially on the tail and undertail.
Blue wing patch (speculum) with white borders that may be narrower than a Mallard's.
Male bill bright yellow; female's dull olive to orange.
Length about 50-58 cm.
Compared with the mallard (female): Mexican Duck is somewhat darker, especially on the tail and undertail, with narrower white wing-patch borders.
Compared with the mottled duck: NatureServe notes difficulty separating Mexican Duck from Mottled Duck may be reducing detection of one or both.

habitat.text: Mostly shallow freshwater marshes of lakes and ponds, slow lowland rivers and irrigated farmland.

behavior.text: Not truly migratory; seasonal local movements, gathering at permanent lakes and rivers in dry seasons and spreading out in rainy seasons
Forages in water by dabbling, head-and-neck submerging or up-ending, rarely diving; also grazes and grubs on land
Mostly plant material (seeds, stems, roots, waste grain), also insects, crustaceans, mollusks and tadpoles
Male gives a thin rreeb; female quacks loudly

resources.title: Black-bellied whistling-duck
resources.description: Identify the black-bellied whistling-duck (Dendrocygna autumnalis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Black-bellied whistling-duck (Dendrocygna autumnalis): Long-necked and long-legged, chestnut, gray and black, with a bright pink bill. Large white wing patch striking in flight. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Resident from southern Arizona and southeastern Texas south through Middle and South America; possibly expanding into eastern Texas and southwestern Louisiana; small flocks may wander well north of the normal range.

rangeSummary.value: Resident from southern Arizona and southeastern Texas south through Middle and South America; possibly expanding into eastern Texas and southwestern Louisiana; small flocks may wander well north of the normal range.

identification.text: Long-necked and long-legged, chestnut, gray and black, with a bright pink bill.
Large white wing patch striking in flight.
Length about 47-51 cm.
Sexes similar; young have a gray bill and muted colours.

habitat.text: Shallow ponds and fresh marshes, favoring ponds surrounded by trees; forages in dry fields and irrigated land.

behavior.text: Gregarious; not strongly migratory, and flocks disappear from some northern breeding areas in winter
Forages much on land, by day or night, on waste grain in harvested fields and on prairies; wades or dabbles in shallow water
Eats mostly seeds and grains; invertebrates under 10% of diet
Mellow whistling calls; nests in tree cavities, nest boxes or on the ground, often in colonies

resources.title: Fulvous whistling-duck
resources.description: Identify the fulvous whistling-duck (Dendrocygna bicolor), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Fulvous whistling-duck (Dendrocygna bicolor): Butterscotch-coloured with a gray bill, long neck and white stripes on the flanks. In flight, black underwings and a white crescent above the tail contrast with the buff body. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds in southern California, southwestern Arizona, central and eastern Texas, Gulf Coast Louisiana and locally southern Florida, south to central Mexico; also breeds in Hawaii (Oahu) and in South America, Africa and India. Spread east along the Gulf Coast from about 1950.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds in southern California, southwestern Arizona, central and eastern Texas, Gulf Coast Louisiana and locally southern Florida, south to central Mexico; also breeds in Hawaii (Oahu) and in South America, Africa and India. Spread east along the Gulf Coast from about 1950.

identification.text: Butterscotch-coloured with a gray bill, long neck and white stripes on the flanks.
In flight, black underwings and a white crescent above the tail contrast with the buff body.
Length about 45-53 cm.
Sexes similar.
Compared with the black-bellied whistling-duck (young): Audubon says to compare young Black-bellied with Fulvous; Fulvous is uniformly butterscotch with a gray bill and white flank stripes.
Compared with the northern pintail (female): Audubon lists female Northern Pintail for comparison; Fulvous has a long neck, white flank stripes and the white rump crescent.

habitat.text: Fresh or brackish marshes in flat open country of the coastal plain, flooded rice fields, other agricultural fields, ponds and lakes.

behavior.text: Regular migration by some Gulf Coast birds to southern Mexico, overshadowed by widespread wandering; flocks have strayed to at least six Canadian provinces
Feeds in water by dabbling or tipping up, sometimes diving; much foraging in damp fields, especially rice fields
Diet more than 95% plant material, mainly seeds of aquatic plants and grasses
Hoarse whistle, ka-wheee

resources.title: Muscovy duck
resources.description: Identify the muscovy duck (Cairina moschata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata): Very large, 64-86 cm, and mostly black. White wing patches obvious in flight, not when swimming. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Wild birds are native from northeastern Mexico south to South America, with small numbers on the Rio Grande in southern Texas. Most Muscovies in North America are barnyard-type birds, and U.S. records probably pertain to escapes or unsuccessful introductions (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: Native in south Texas; feral elsewhere

rangeSummary.value: Wild birds are native from northeastern Mexico south to South America, with small numbers on the Rio Grande in southern Texas. Most Muscovies in North America are barnyard-type birds, and U.S. records probably pertain to escapes or unsuccessful introductions (NatureServe).

identification.text: Very large, 64-86 cm, and mostly black.
White wing patches obvious in flight, not when swimming.
Male larger and glossier than female, with a knob above the bill.
Domesticated forms usually have much white in the plumage.

habitat.text: Wooded rivers and swamps in the wild; domestic-type birds around ponds and urban and suburban waters.

behavior.text: Wild birds are wary, fast-flying birds of wooded rivers and swamps
Nests in tree cavities and will use nest boxes
Not often heard; quiet quacks and grunts

resources.title: Eurasian wigeon
resources.description: Identify the eurasian wigeon (Mareca penelope), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eurasian wigeon (Mareca penelope): Male: bright rusty head with buff crown stripe and mostly gray body. Female very much like female American Wigeon, may have a browner head. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds in Eurasia. In North America winters on the Pacific coast from southeastern Alaska to northern Baja California and on the Atlantic-Gulf coast from Labrador and Newfoundland to Florida and southern Texas.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it was formerly placed in Anas (AOU 1983, 1998) and is now treated in Mareca on genetic evidence (AOU 2017).
Regular visitor; taken under general duck bags

rangeSummary.value: Breeds in Eurasia. In North America winters on the Pacific coast from southeastern Alaska to northern Baja California and on the Atlantic-Gulf coast from Labrador and Newfoundland to Florida and southern Texas.

identification.text: Male: bright rusty head with buff crown stripe and mostly gray body.
Female very much like female American Wigeon, may have a browner head.
Rare hybrids with American Wigeon show intermediate patterns (American Wigeon can also have buff on the crown).
Length about 42-54 cm.
Compared with the american wigeon: Female is very much alike; Eurasian may have a browner head. Hybrids are rare and intermediate.

habitat.text: Marshes, lakes, bays and fields; in winter often marshy ponds with open ground nearby, flooded fields, shallow coastal estuaries and sheltered bays. American Wigeon presence is the best key to good habitat.

behavior.text: Reaches North America from both east and west; Pacific-lowland winterers probably come from eastern Siberia
Forages by grazing on land, dabbling, or sometimes submerging head and neck; may steal food brought up by coots or geese; feeds day or night
Piping two-note whistle, seldom heard in America

resources.title: Egyptian goose
resources.description: Identify the egyptian goose (Alopochen aegyptiaca), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Egyptian goose (Alopochen aegyptiaca): Heavy-bodied goose, 63-76 cm, mostly shades of tan and brown. Dark neck ring and black eye patch. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to sub-Saharan Africa and the Nile Valley. Escaped birds have established wild populations in Florida (largest), Texas and California, mostly in urban and suburban areas.

taxonomicNotes.text: Listed only as unprotected where audited; unprotected status alone does not establish a hunting opportunity

rangeSummary.value: Native to sub-Saharan Africa and the Nile Valley. Escaped birds have established wild populations in Florida (largest), Texas and California, mostly in urban and suburban areas.

identification.text: Heavy-bodied goose, 63-76 cm, mostly shades of tan and brown.
Dark neck ring and black eye patch.
Big white patches on black wings striking in flight.
Sexes similar; male slightly larger.

habitat.text: Freshwater wetlands, lakes, ponds and rivers, and urban and suburban habitats; mostly urban and suburban areas in North America (USFWS quoting Braun 2004).

behavior.text: Non-native; will not populate densely wooded areas, found in meadows, grasslands, agricultural fields and around rivers, lakes, ponds and wetlands (USFWS, citing Tattan 2004)
Aggressive toward other bird species, which may keep smaller species from establishing territories (USFWS ERSS)

resources.title: Emperor goose
resources.description: Identify the emperor goose (Anser canagicus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Emperor goose (Anser canagicus): Gray body with white head, black foreneck and chin, and scaly pattern on the body; length 66-71 cm. Blue-morph Snow Goose is somewhat similar but lacks the black foreneck and scaly pattern. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: More than 90 percent of the breeding population nests in the eastern Bering Sea region of western Alaska (Kuskokwim Bay to Kotzebue Sound), with small numbers in eastern Asia. Most winter in the Aleutian Islands; autumn strays reach Oregon and California.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it was formerly placed in Chen and, by AOU (1983), in the monotypic genus Philacte; it is now placed in Anser (AOU 2017).

rangeSummary.value: More than 90 percent of the breeding population nests in the eastern Bering Sea region of western Alaska (Kuskokwim Bay to Kotzebue Sound), with small numbers in eastern Asia. Most winter in the Aleutian Islands; autumn strays reach Oregon and California.

identification.text: Gray body with white head, black foreneck and chin, and scaly pattern on the body; length 66-71 cm.
Blue-morph Snow Goose is somewhat similar but lacks the black foreneck and scaly pattern.
Juvenile in first fall has an all-dark head, neck and bill.
Loud musical call, kla-ha, kla-ha, kla-ha.
Compared with the snow goose (blue morph): Emperor Goose has a black foreneck and chin and a scaly body pattern; the blue morph has a gray body and white head without them.

habitat.text: Summer on tundra, mostly low marshy tundra within 10 miles of coast; winter on rocky shores and mudflats. Closely tied to salt water at all seasons.

behavior.text: Short-distance migrant, often in large flocks; stages for weeks on large lagoons on the north shore of the Alaska Peninsula
On breeding grounds forages on land, grubbing roots and grazing fresh growth; in migration and winter feeds on mudflats exposed by falling tides
Diet is plant material in summer (roots, bulbs, sedges, crowberry or blueberry) and clams, mussels and marine algae in migration and winter

resources.title: Clapper rail
resources.description: Identify the clapper rail (Rallus crepitans), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Clapper rail (Rallus crepitans): Chicken-sized (35-48 cm) with a long narrow bill and barring on the flanks. Underparts vary from buffy gray on the Atlantic Coast to dull cinnamon on the Gulf Coast. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coasts of the western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean: Massachusetts south through Florida along the Atlantic, and Florida west to Tamaulipas along the Gulf.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats Rallus crepitans as a species; it notes older treatments considered it conspecific with King Rail (AOU 1998), and that Pacific-coast and Colorado River populations have been variously treated as R. longirostris, R. elegans or R. obsoletus (AOU 1983).

rangeSummary.value: Coasts of the western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean: Massachusetts south through Florida along the Atlantic, and Florida west to Tamaulipas along the Gulf.

identification.text: Chicken-sized (35-48 cm) with a long narrow bill and barring on the flanks.
Underparts vary from buffy gray on the Atlantic Coast to dull cinnamon on the Gulf Coast.
Juvenile darker and duller.
Almost never seen away from salt marsh.

habitat.text: Salt marsh, rarely brackish; strictly salt marsh along most of the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, sometimes adjacent brackish marsh, and shallow mangrove swamps in Florida.

behavior.text: Harsh clattering call, kek-kek-kek-kek-kek
Forages by walking in shallow water or on mud, especially on a falling or low tide, taking prey from the ground or vegetation or probing
Eats mainly crustaceans (crabs, crayfish), also aquatic insects, small fish, mollusks, worms, frogs and sometimes seeds
Found year-round in many parts of its range; some withdrawal from the northern Atlantic end in winter

resources.title: Double-crested cormorant
resources.description: Identify the double-crested cormorant (Nannopterum auritum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Double-crested cormorant (Nannopterum auritum): Blackish all over with orange bare skin on the face and throat extending to the lores; 76-89 cm. Breeding western birds show white head tufts, absent on eastern birds. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from southeastern Bering Sea and southern Alaska and from southern British Columbia east through Manitoba to coastal Quebec and Newfoundland, south to Baja California, the Gulf Coast, Florida and Belize; breeding range has expanded.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe uses Nannopterum auritum (AOS 2021); Nannopterum was formerly synonymized with Phalacrocorax (AOU 1983, 1998), so older sources call it Phalacrocorax auritus.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from southeastern Bering Sea and southern Alaska and from southern British Columbia east through Manitoba to coastal Quebec and Newfoundland, south to Baja California, the Gulf Coast, Florida and Belize; breeding range has expanded.

identification.text: Blackish all over with orange bare skin on the face and throat extending to the lores; 76-89 cm.
Breeding western birds show white head tufts, absent on eastern birds.
Immatures brownish, paler on the foreneck and chest, often fading to whitish there.
In flight the neck is held with a slight crook behind the head; most cormorants look straight-necked.
Compared with the great cormorant: Larger and bulkier with a broad white band across the throat, dull yellow (not orange) throat pouch and, when breeding, white flank patches.

habitat.text: Very adaptable; almost any aquatic habitat from rocky northern coasts to mangrove swamps, large reservoirs and small inland ponds.

behavior.text: Forages by diving from the surface and swimming underwater propelled by the feet, singly or in groups
Eats a wide variety of fish, also crabs, shrimp, crayfish, frogs, salamanders and eels
Deep guttural grunts; nests in trees near or over water, on sea cliffs or on island ground
Most are migratory, in flocks often following coastlines or rivers

resources.title: Great cormorant
resources.description: Identify the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo): Large and bulky, 84-100 cm, with a relatively short tail, big head and thick bill. Adult has a broad white band across the throat behind bare yellow face skin; breeding birds show white flank patches. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: In North America breeds along the Atlantic coast from the Gulf of St. Lawrence and southwestern Newfoundland to Nova Scotia (recolonized Maine); winters from the breeding range south to North Carolina, sometimes farther. Also Iceland, southwestern Greenland and much of the Old World.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it was regarded as conspecific with African P. lucidus by AOU (1983, 1998) and forms a superspecies with P. capillatus.

rangeSummary.value: In North America breeds along the Atlantic coast from the Gulf of St. Lawrence and southwestern Newfoundland to Nova Scotia (recolonized Maine); winters from the breeding range south to North Carolina, sometimes farther. Also Iceland, southwestern Greenland and much of the Old World.

identification.text: Large and bulky, 84-100 cm, with a relatively short tail, big head and thick bill.
Adult has a broad white band across the throat behind bare yellow face skin; breeding birds show white flank patches.
Immature brownish, resembling Double-crested Cormorant but usually with brown neck and chest contrasting with a white belly.
Throat pouch dull yellow, not orange.
Compared with the double-crested cormorant: Smaller; orange throat pouch and no broad white throat band or white flank patches.

habitat.text: Mainly coastal, over shallow waters close to shore, especially sheltered bays; nests on sea cliffs. In the Old World regularly far inland on lakes, rivers and swamps.

behavior.text: Migrates in flocks, paralleling the coastline a short distance offshore
Most foraging within 10 ft of the surface, diving to about 30 ft; feeds almost entirely on fish
Nests on rocky cliffs of coasts and islands; wintering birds often around rock jetties and recently on large inland rivers

resources.title: Thick-billed murre
resources.description: Identify the thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia): About 46 cm, much like Common Murre. Slightly thicker bill with a white mark at the gape when seen close. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds on islands and coasts in the Arctic of North America and Eurasia, south to the Aleutians and Kodiak, Hudson Bay and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Newfoundland waters are the most important western Atlantic wintering area; regular in winter off New England.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds on islands and coasts in the Arctic of North America and Eurasia, south to the Aleutians and Kodiak, Hudson Bay and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Newfoundland waters are the most important western Atlantic wintering area; regular in winter off New England.

identification.text: About 46 cm, much like Common Murre.
Slightly thicker bill with a white mark at the gape when seen close.
Blacker back (hard to see without direct comparison).
In summer may show white coming up higher in a point on the chest; in winter may show more black on the face than Common Murre.
Compared with the common murre: Slightly thinner bill without the white gape mark; less black on the face in winter; avoids pack-ice areas.

habitat.text: Ocean, favoring very cold Arctic waters and often far from land over deep water when not nesting; associates with edges of pack ice; nests on rocky coasts and islands with steep cliffs.

behavior.text: Nests colonially on ledges of sea-cliff; some remain through winter as far north as open water allows, including around openings in pack ice, others move south
Forages swimming underwater, diving more than 200 ft; eats mostly fish (cod, herring, capelin, sand lance) with more crustaceans in winter
Low purring murrrr, plus croaks and growls at breeding colonies

resources.title: Common murre
resources.description: Identify the common murre (Uria aalge), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common murre (Uria aalge): Charcoal above and white below, sharply two-toned in summer with more white on the face in winter. Length about 40-45 cm. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds along North Pacific coasts from the Bering Strait south to central California and the North Atlantic from western Greenland and Iceland south to Newfoundland; some birds reach New England waters and southern California in winter.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds along North Pacific coasts from the Bering Strait south to central California and the North Atlantic from western Greenland and Iceland south to Newfoundland; some birds reach New England waters and southern California in winter.

identification.text: Charcoal above and white below, sharply two-toned in summer with more white on the face in winter.
Length about 40-45 cm.
Similar Thick-billed Murre is very close; compare to loons.
Compared with the thick-billed murre: Slightly thicker bill with a white mark at the gape, blacker back, and often more black on the face in winter.

habitat.text: Ocean and large bays, favoring cool waters over the continental shelf, offshore and rather near the coast; tends to avoid pack ice.

behavior.text: Purring or murmuring call (hence the name), plus a guttural croak and higher bleat
Forages swimming underwater, diving over 150 ft; eats herring, cod, capelin, sand lance and other fish, plus crustaceans, worms and squid
Nests on cliff ledges and flat bare rock atop sea stacks; permanent resident in many areas but must leave northern western-Alaska colonies when waters freeze

resources.title: Common raven
resources.description: Identify the common raven (Corvus corax), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common raven (Corvus corax): Much larger than crows: 56-69 cm, wingspan about 116-118 cm. Wedge-shaped tail, very thick bill and shaggy throat feathers. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Resident from northernmost North America south to southern Baja California, Nicaragua and Texas, and east of the Rockies to southern Saskatchewan, northeastern Minnesota, northern Michigan and southern New England; also Greenland, Iceland and the Old World.

rangeSummary.value: Resident from northernmost North America south to southern Baja California, Nicaragua and Texas, and east of the Rockies to southern Saskatchewan, northeastern Minnesota, northern Michigan and southern New England; also Greenland, Iceland and the Old World.

identification.text: Much larger than crows: 56-69 cm, wingspan about 116-118 cm.
Wedge-shaped tail, very thick bill and shaggy throat feathers.
Deep, varied, guttural croaking; a hollow wonk-wonk.
In the Southwest, compare to Chihuahuan Raven.
Compared with the chihuahuan raven: Audubon says to compare it in the Southwest but gives no separating marks.

habitat.text: Boreal and mountain forests, coastal cliffs, tundra and desert; may also live on prairies if suitable nest sites such as cliffs are nearby.

behavior.text: Mostly a permanent resident; some wander in fall and winter south of the breeding range
Typically forages in pairs, sometimes cooperating to flush prey; mostly forages on the ground
Omnivorous opportunist: carrion, garbage, insects, rodents, lizards, frogs and eggs and young of other birds

resources.title: Black-billed magpie
resources.description: Identify the black-billed magpie (Pica hudsonia), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Black-billed magpie (Pica hudsonia): Unmistakable in most areas; 45-60 cm. Green and blue gloss on the wings and long tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Resident from south-coastal and southern Alaska through western Canada to eastern California, southern Nevada and Utah, northern New Mexico and western Kansas and Oklahoma.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it was formerly included in the Eurasian Magpie (Pica pica) and was split on morphological, behavioural and genetic characters (AOU 2000); some authors consider it conspecific with Yellow-billed Magpie.

rangeSummary.value: Resident from south-coastal and southern Alaska through western Canada to eastern California, southern Nevada and Utah, northern New Mexico and western Kansas and Oklahoma.

identification.text: Unmistakable in most areas; 45-60 cm.
Green and blue gloss on the wings and long tail.
Big white wing patches flash in flight.
In California, see Yellow-billed Magpie.
Compared with the yellow-billed magpie: Found in California; the Black-billed has a black bill (Audubon says to see Yellow-billed there).

habitat.text: Semi-open country in the west: rangeland, conifers, streamsides, forest edges and farms; most common in streamside groves in open terrain. Avoids unbroken forest, treeless grasslands and extreme desert.

behavior.text: Mostly a permanent resident, with some upslope movement in fall and a few moving south or downslope in winter
Forages mostly by walking on the ground, flipping items with the bill; may take ticks from elk and other animals
Omnivorous, eating more insects than most crows plus carrion, rodents, eggs and nestlings, with more berries, seeds and nuts in winter
Rapid, nasal mag? mag? mag? or yak yak yak

resources.title: European starling
resources.description: Identify the european starling (Sturnus vulgaris), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: European starling (Sturnus vulgaris): Short tail and thin straight bill; 20.6-23.1 cm. Black with purple and green gloss in spring and summer. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to Eurasia; introduced in New York City in 1890. Now breeds from southeastern Alaska across southern Canada and south through most of the U.S. to southern Mexico.

rangeSummary.value: Native to Eurasia; introduced in New York City in 1890. Now breeds from southeastern Alaska across southern Canada and south through most of the U.S. to southern Mexico.

identification.text: Short tail and thin straight bill; 20.6-23.1 cm.
Black with purple and green gloss in spring and summer.
Fresh fall plumage heavily marked with white spots, wearing off through winter.
Bill bright yellow in breeding season (base of lower mandible blue in males, pink in females), duller otherwise.
Juveniles all dusty gray with dark bills.

habitat.text: Cities, parks, farms, open groves and fields; almost any disturbed habitat, usually scarce in extensive wild forest, scrub or desert.

behavior.text: Usually forages in flocks, mostly on the ground probing soil; sometimes takes fruit in trees or insects in the air
Mostly insects, berries and seeds; often imitates other birds
Northern birds mostly move south in fall, migrating by day; southern birds may be permanent residents

resources.title: House sparrow
resources.description: Identify the house sparrow (Passer domesticus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: House sparrow (Passer domesticus): 13-17 cm. Male: black bib, white cheeks, gray crown and chestnut nape. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to the Old World; introduced and established from the north coast of British Columbia and southern Yukon to Newfoundland and south beyond North America.

rangeSummary.value: Native to the Old World; introduced and established from the north coast of British Columbia and southern Yukon to Newfoundland and south beyond North America.

identification.text: Male: black bib, white cheeks, gray crown and chestnut nape.
Female: pale buff eyebrow, plain gray chest, black and buff stripes on a brown back.

habitat.text: Cities, towns and farms; in North America essentially always around manmade structures, never in unaltered natural habitats.

behavior.text: Forages mostly hopping on the ground; will perch on weed stalks for seeds and search car fronts and bark for insects
Mostly weed and grass seeds and waste grain, also insects in summer and human food scraps in cities
Shrill, monotonous, noisy chirping; permanent resident

resources.title: Red-winged blackbird
resources.description: Identify the red-winged blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Red-winged blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus): Male: black with bright red shoulder patches (epaulets), typically bordered with yellow; patches can be concealed by body feathers. Female and young: streaky brown with a buff eyebrow; can resemble sparrows but differ in behavior, have a spikier bill and darker lower belly. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from southern Yukon across Canada to Nova Scotia and south through the U.S. and Central America to Costa Rica; winters over much of the U.S., especially the south.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes two groups: phoeniceus (Red-winged) and gubernator (Bicolored Blackbird, of the Mexican Plateau); Audubon notes birds in central California with entirely red shoulder patches are called Bicolored Blackbird.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from southern Yukon across Canada to Nova Scotia and south through the U.S. and Central America to Costa Rica; winters over much of the U.S., especially the south.

identification.text: Male: black with bright red shoulder patches (epaulets), typically bordered with yellow; patches can be concealed by body feathers.
Female and young: streaky brown with a buff eyebrow; can resemble sparrows but differ in behavior, have a spikier bill and darker lower belly.
Length 17-23 cm.

habitat.text: Breeds in marshes, brushy swamps and hayfields; forages in cultivated land and along water edges; in the non-breeding season flocks gather in farm fields, pastures and feedlots.

behavior.text: Males arrive before females in spring in the north; migrates in flocks and is present year-round in many areas
Forages mostly walking on the ground, in flocks with other blackbirds and starlings outside the breeding season
Mostly insects and seeds (about three-quarters of the annual diet is seeds)
Song a rich, musical o-ka-leeee!

resources.title: Yellow-headed blackbird
resources.description: Identify the yellow-headed blackbird (Xanthocephalus xanthocephalus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Yellow-headed blackbird (Xanthocephalus xanthocephalus): Male: black with a yellow head and white wing patches that stand out in flight. Female: smaller, sooty brown with yellow on the face and chest, white streaks on the belly and no white wing patches. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from central-interior British Columbia east to extreme western Ontario and northwestern Ohio, south to southern California, New Mexico and northern Texas; winters from central California, Arizona and Texas south into Mexico.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from central-interior British Columbia east to extreme western Ontario and northwestern Ohio, south to southern California, New Mexico and northern Texas; winters from central California, Arizona and Texas south into Mexico.

identification.text: Male: black with a yellow head and white wing patches that stand out in flight.
Female: smaller, sooty brown with yellow on the face and chest, white streaks on the belly and no white wing patches.
Immatures have some yellow on the head and small or absent wing patches.
Length 21-26 cm.

habitat.text: Breeds in freshwater sloughs, marshy lake borders and tall cattails in water up to 3-4 ft deep; forages around marshes and in pastures, plowed fields and feedlots.

behavior.text: Migrates in flocks; males may winter farther north than females
Forages mostly walking in open fields or at water edges; may follow farm machinery; usually in flocks with other blackbirds outside nesting
Feeds heavily on insects in summer; about two-thirds of diet is seeds
Harsh, incessant oka-wee-wee and kruck calls that blend into a wavering chorus in colonies

resources.title: Brewer's blackbird
resources.description: Identify the brewer's blackbird (Euphagus cyanocephalus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Brewer's blackbird (Euphagus cyanocephalus): Male: all glossy black with whitish eyes; female dull gray-brown with dark eyes. Shorter-tailed than Common Grackle and a bit larger than Brown-headed Cowbird. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from central interior British Columbia to the western Great Lakes, south to northwestern Baja California, Nevada, Texas and northern Iowa; present year-round in parts of the western U.S. and winters east to the southeastern U.S. and Mexico.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from central interior British Columbia to the western Great Lakes, south to northwestern Baja California, Nevada, Texas and northern Iowa; present year-round in parts of the western U.S. and winters east to the southeastern U.S. and Mexico.

identification.text: Male: all glossy black with whitish eyes; female dull gray-brown with dark eyes.
Shorter-tailed than Common Grackle and a bit larger than Brown-headed Cowbird.
Length 21-25 cm.
Compared with the rusty blackbird: Rusty is less glossy with a thinner bill, yellow eyes and, in fall, rusty feather edges.
Compared with the common grackle: Longer-tailed than Brewer's.
Compared with the brown-headed cowbird: A bit smaller than Brewer's.

habitat.text: Open and semi-open country: fields, prairies, farms, parks, shrubby areas near water; often around human habitations including suburban lawns and parking lots.

behavior.text: Walks on the ground searching for food, sometimes wading or catching insects in flight; may follow farm machinery
Usually forages in flocks except when nesting
Insects (grasshoppers, crickets, beetles), seeds, waste grain and berries
Gurgles, squawks and whistles

resources.title: Rusty blackbird
resources.description: Identify the rusty blackbird (Euphagus carolinus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Rusty blackbird (Euphagus carolinus): Male dull black, female slaty, with yellow eyes in most seasons; 21-25 cm. Like male Brewer's Blackbird but less glossy, with a thinner bill. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from Alaska to Labrador and south to central British Columbia, northern Great Lakes, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine and Nova Scotia; in the non-breeding season ranges south to Texas, the Gulf Coast and northern Florida, primarily the southeastern U.S. Assessed Special Concern in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe recognizes two subspecies: E. c. carolinus and the darker E. c. nigrans, which breeds in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Magdalen Island and possibly eastern New Brunswick.
A declining species; current federal depredation coverage not verified

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from Alaska to Labrador and south to central British Columbia, northern Great Lakes, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine and Nova Scotia; in the non-breeding season ranges south to Texas, the Gulf Coast and northern Florida, primarily the southeastern U.S. Assessed Special Concern in Canada.

identification.text: Male dull black, female slaty, with yellow eyes in most seasons; 21-25 cm.
Like male Brewer's Blackbird but less glossy, with a thinner bill.
In fall distinctive with rusty feather edges and a buff eyebrow.
Compared with the brewer's blackbird: Brewer's male is glossier with a thicker bill; ranges mainly west of Rusty's range.
Compared with the common grackle: Longer-tailed and larger.

habitat.text: Breeds in wet northern coniferous forest and muskeg with many lakes and bogs; in migration and winter favors trees near water such as wooded swamps and riverside forest, and forages in fields and feedlots. Canadian sources describe breeding near wetlands: sedge meadows, beaver ponds, muskegs and shrub-riparian areas.

behavior.text: Migrates relatively late in fall and early in spring; strays appear in the West and Southwest most often in late fall
Forages mostly walking on wet ground or wading in shallow water, alone or in flocks, sometimes joining other blackbirds in dry fields
Mostly insects including aquatic ones (caddisflies, mayflies, dragonflies), also snails, crustaceans, small fish and salamanders, and seeds and waste grain in winter
Song like the squeaks of a rusty gate; call a sharp check

resources.title: Brown-headed cowbird
resources.description: Identify the brown-headed cowbird (Molothrus ater), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Brown-headed cowbird (Molothrus ater): Male: glossy black with a contrasting brown head. Female: plain dusty brown with a dark, sparrowlike bill. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from southeast Alaska, northern British Columbia and southern Mackenzie to Newfoundland, south to central Mexico, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida; winters from the northern U.S. south.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from southeast Alaska, northern British Columbia and southern Mackenzie to Newfoundland, south to central Mexico, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida; winters from the northern U.S. south.

identification.text: Male: glossy black with a contrasting brown head.
Female: plain dusty brown with a dark, sparrowlike bill.
Juvenile streaked at first.
Male 19-22 cm, female 15-20 cm.

habitat.text: Open or semi-open country year-round: farms, fields, prairies, wood edges and river groves; in winter concentrates in farmland, pastures and feedlots.

behavior.text: Forages mostly walking on the ground, often with cattle or horses catching flushed insects; originally associated with bison herds
Seeds are about half of the summer diet and over 90% in winter; the rest mostly insects
Migrants may begin leaving nesting areas by July or August; present all year in many southern areas
Squeaky gurgle; call is a check or rattle

resources.title: Bronzed cowbird
resources.description: Identify the bronzed cowbird (Molothrus aeneus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Bronzed cowbird (Molothrus aeneus): Larger than Brown-headed Cowbird, with a longer bill and shorter tail. Red eyes (hard to see); neck ruff gives a hunched-shoulder look. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Resident from extreme southeastern California, Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and western and southern Texas south to Panama; northern populations partially migratory.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it is composed of two groups formerly considered separate species, aeneus (Bronzed) and armenti (Bronze-brown, South America), and is often placed in genus Tangavius (AOU 1998).

rangeSummary.value: Resident from extreme southeastern California, Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and western and southern Texas south to Panama; northern populations partially migratory.

identification.text: Larger than Brown-headed Cowbird, with a longer bill and shorter tail.
Red eyes (hard to see); neck ruff gives a hunched-shoulder look.
Females dull black in Texas or gray-brown in Arizona.
Length 18-20 cm.
Compared with the brown-headed cowbird: Bronzed is larger with a longer bill, shorter tail, red eye and neck ruff.

habitat.text: Farmland, brush, semi-open country and feedlots; outside breeding generally very open lowland habitats, roosting in brushy woods.

behavior.text: Only a short-distance migrant; very uncommon and local in the Southwest in winter, some stray east along the Gulf Coast to Florida
Forages mostly walking on the ground in the open, sometimes with cattle or horses; may take ticks or insects from cattle backs
Diet is largely seeds and waste grain, plus insects, snails and spiders; snails may supply calcium to laying females

resources.title: Shiny cowbird
resources.description: Identify the shiny cowbird (Molothrus bonariensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Shiny cowbird (Molothrus bonariensis): Male black all over with shiny purple gloss. Much like Brown-headed Cowbird in size and shape; females not safely identified. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Resident from eastern Panama south to central Chile and Argentina; expanded through the Caribbean during the 1900s, reaching Puerto Rico in 1955; in North America occurs mostly in southern Florida.

rangeSummary.value: Resident from eastern Panama south to central Chile and Argentina; expanded through the Caribbean during the 1900s, reaching Puerto Rico in 1955; in North America occurs mostly in southern Florida.

identification.text: Male black all over with shiny purple gloss.
Much like Brown-headed Cowbird in size and shape; females not safely identified.
Most other all-black birds are either much larger or have pale eyes.
Length 18-20 cm.
Compared with the brown-headed cowbird: Similar in size and shape; the male Shiny is entirely black with purple gloss, and females are not safely separated.

habitat.text: Semi-open country; in North America mostly near the coast, often foraging on extensive lawns.

behavior.text: Migration within North America poorly known; spring numbers move through southern Florida, and strays have reached Texas, Oklahoma and Maine
Forages mostly walking on the ground in open areas, often in small flocks with other cowbirds or blackbirds
Melodious warble song and harsh metallic call notes

resources.title: Common grackle
resources.description: Identify the common grackle (Quiscalus quiscula), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common grackle (Quiscalus quiscula): Male glossy black with an iridescent bluish or purplish head, neck and breast; female less glossy. Long tail with a crease down the middle, whitish-yellow eyes, strong bill; 28-34 cm. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds from northeastern British Columbia and southern Mackenzie to Newfoundland, south to southern Texas, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida, west to Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico; winters from Kansas, the southern Great Lakes and New England south.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it is composed of two groups formerly considered separate species, quiscula (Purple Grackle) and versicolor (Bronzed Grackle); studies disagree on whether they are conspecific.

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from northeastern British Columbia and southern Mackenzie to Newfoundland, south to southern Texas, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida, west to Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico; winters from Kansas, the southern Great Lakes and New England south.

identification.text: Male glossy black with an iridescent bluish or purplish head, neck and breast; female less glossy.
Long tail with a crease down the middle, whitish-yellow eyes, strong bill; 28-34 cm.
Bronzed form: bronzy body contrasts with blue-black head; Purple form of the southeast has purple and green gloss with less contrast.
Juveniles have dark eyes; molting birds in late summer have short or ragged tails.
Compared with the great-tailed grackle: Larger with a much longer tail and more evenly coloured male.
Compared with the rusty blackbird: Smaller, with a shorter tail and thinner bill.

habitat.text: Open or semi-open country: farmland, towns, groves and streamsides; forages in farm fields, pastures, suburban lawns, feedlots and marshes.

behavior.text: Migrates in flocks by day; partial migrant, present all year in much of the eastern U.S.
Forages walking or wading, also up in trees and shrubs, usually in flocks when not nesting; sometimes steals food from other birds
Omnivorous: mostly grains and seeds in winter and migration, insects in summer, also crayfish, minnows, frogs, eggs and young of other birds
Nests and roosts in dense trees, especially conifers, near open areas

resources.title: Great-tailed grackle
resources.description: Identify the great-tailed grackle (Quiscalus mexicanus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Great-tailed grackle (Quiscalus mexicanus): Very long tail and yellow eyes; male 46-58 cm, female 38-46 cm. Male glossy black, more evenly coloured than Common Grackle and much larger. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Resident from southeastern California and southern Nevada east to southern Nebraska and southwestern Missouri, south into South America; breeding range is expanding, with recent nesting in Oregon and probably Idaho.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it was formerly considered conspecific with Boat-tailed Grackle (Q. major), but sympatry without interbreeding is known from Louisiana to Texas (AOU 1998).

rangeSummary.value: Resident from southeastern California and southern Nevada east to southern Nebraska and southwestern Missouri, south into South America; breeding range is expanding, with recent nesting in Oregon and probably Idaho.

identification.text: Very long tail and yellow eyes; male 46-58 cm, female 38-46 cm.
Male glossy black, more evenly coloured than Common Grackle and much larger.
Female buff below and on the eyebrow, smaller than the male.
Compare to Boat-tailed Grackle.
Compared with the common grackle: Smaller with a shorter tail and less evenly coloured male.
Compared with the boat-tailed grackle: Audubon says to compare; NatureServe treats it as a separate species with overlap from Louisiana to Texas.

habitat.text: Groves, thickets, farms, towns and city parks; mostly lowlands including farmland, marshes, irrigated fields, suburban lawns and brushy areas; avoids true desert but occurs around streams or ponds in dry country.

behavior.text: Usually feeds in flocks, mostly on the ground or wading in very shallow water; also forages in trees and shrubs, searching for nests to rob
Omnivorous: insects, spiders, crayfish, tadpoles, small fish, lizards, eggs and nestlings, plus seeds, waste grain, berries and fruit
Variety of whistles, clucks and hissing notes; breeding range is expanding

resources.title: Boat-tailed grackle
resources.description: Identify the boat-tailed grackle (Quiscalus major), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Boat-tailed grackle (Quiscalus major): Male 38-50 cm with a long, rounded, wedge-shaped tail; entirely dark. Female much smaller (27-34 cm) than the male. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal eastern US from Long Island and New Jersey south through peninsular Florida and west along the Gulf coast to southeastern Texas; absent from the western Florida Panhandle. Not a Canadian species.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it was formerly treated as conspecific with the great-tailed grackle (Q. mexicanus) and is often placed in genus Cassidix.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal eastern US from Long Island and New Jersey south through peninsular Florida and west along the Gulf coast to southeastern Texas; absent from the western Florida Panhandle. Not a Canadian species.

identification.text: Male 38-50 cm with a long, rounded, wedge-shaped tail; entirely dark.
Female much smaller (27-34 cm) than the male.
Iris yellow from northeast Florida north; dark on the Texas-Louisiana coast (young great-tailed grackles also have dark eyes).
Call is a harsh repeated 'jeeb', unlike the whistles and clucks of the great-tailed grackle.
Compared with the great-tailed grackle: Slightly longer-tailed and less round-headed; whistles and clucks rather than harsh jeebs.
Compared with the common grackle: Audubon points to it for identification in areas north of northeast Florida where boat-tailed has yellow eyes.

habitat.text: Marshes, beaches and coastal areas, almost always near water; inland only in Florida, generally near marshes and lakes.

behavior.text: Forages by walking on shore or in shallow water and steals food from larger birds
