Nests in noisy colonies near water; males display with wing-fluttering and harsh calls
Mostly a permanent resident

resources.title: Steller's eider
resources.description: Identify the steller's eider (Polysticta stelleri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Steller's eider (Polysticta stelleri): Smallest eider, 43-47 cm, square-headed; often floats with tail cocked up. Breeding male: peachy chest, black neck ring and eye spot, green and black crest knob. It is protected; if you are not certain of the species, do not shoot. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds in Arctic Russia and in Alaska (Arctic Coastal Plain and Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta); Alaska and eastern Siberian birds molt and winter mainly along the Alaska Peninsula; some Russian-Atlantic birds winter in Europe.

taxonomicNotes.text: Federally threatened; closed in Alaska

rangeSummary.value: Breeds in Arctic Russia and in Alaska (Arctic Coastal Plain and Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta); Alaska and eastern Siberian birds molt and winter mainly along the Alaska Peninsula; some Russian-Atlantic birds winter in Europe.

identification.text: Smallest eider, 43-47 cm, square-headed; often floats with tail cocked up.
Breeding male: peachy chest, black neck ring and eye spot, green and black crest knob.
Female: plain dark brown, can suggest a female scoter or dabbling duck; note the square head and white-bordered blue wing patch.
Wing patch (speculum) is iridescent blue-purple with white borders in all ages.
Compared with the female scoters: Steller's female has a square head and white-bordered blue wing patch.
Compared with the harlequin duck: Steller's eider associates with harlequin flocks; identify by the wing patch and head shape.

habitat.text: Nests on low tundra near lakes and ponds, often inland; winters at sea near rocky shores or pack-ice edges.

behavior.text: Sociable; flies in tightly packed flocks and feeds in compact groups, dives together
Lone birds may join flocks of harlequin ducks or other divers
Winter diet mostly mollusks and crustaceans; tundra diet mostly aquatic insects
Male has a weak moan; female low growling notes

conservationStatus.text: The Alaska-breeding population is listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act.
The steller's eider, U.S. Alaska breeding population only: listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1997-06-11.

resources.title: Spectacled eider
resources.description: Identify the spectacled eider (Somateria fischeri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Spectacled eider (Somateria fischeri): Male: bold white 'spectacles' around the eye on a green head, black chest and underparts, white back. Female: mottled brown with a hint of the male's face pattern. It is protected; if you are not certain of the species, do not shoot. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds in Arctic Alaska (Beaufort Sea west to Norton Sound and the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta) and eastern Russia; non-breeding in the Bering and Chukchi seas.

taxonomicNotes.text: Federally threatened; closed in Alaska

rangeSummary.value: Breeds in Arctic Alaska (Beaufort Sea west to Norton Sound and the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta) and eastern Russia; non-breeding in the Bering and Chukchi seas.

identification.text: Male: bold white 'spectacles' around the eye on a green head, black chest and underparts, white back.
Female: mottled brown with a hint of the male's face pattern.
Large round eye patch of different colour and texture is present in downy chicks and all plumages.
Common and King eiders have a bill frontal process reaching near the eye; the spectacled eider does not, and its forehead feathering runs far forward to just behind the nostril.
Common eider is distinctly larger and King eider slightly larger than spectacled eider.
Compared with the common eider: Distinctly larger, bill frontal process reaches near the eye, no spectacle patch.
Compared with the king eider: Slightly larger, bill frontal process reaches near the eye, no spectacle patch.

habitat.text: Breeds in wet coastal tundra with shallow ponds; otherwise at sea, often among pack ice.

behavior.text: Small compact flocks; huge dense flocks in openings in sea ice in winter
Dives longer than most diving ducks; eats mollusks and crustaceans at sea
Summer tundra diet includes aquatic insects, sedges, grasses and berries
Migrates offshore over the Bering, Chukchi and Beaufort seas

conservationStatus.text: Listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act.
The spectacled eider, wherever found: listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1993-05-10.

resources.title: Snowy owl
resources.description: Identify the snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus): About 61 cm, bulky and round-headed with yellow eyes; wingspan about 1.4 m. White with variable black barring: young females heavily marked, old males almost pure white. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Breeds on Arctic tundra from Alaska and northern Canada to Labrador; many winter on the northern Great Plains and Prairies, with irregular southward irruptions.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly placed in the monotypic genus Nyctea (still used by Animal Diversity Web); NatureServe places it in Bubo.
Alaska names a resident season; its federal basis is unresolved

rangeSummary.value: Breeds on Arctic tundra from Alaska and northern Canada to Labrador; many winter on the northern Great Plains and Prairies, with irregular southward irruptions.

identification.text: About 61 cm, bulky and round-headed with yellow eyes; wingspan about 1.4 m.
White with variable black barring: young females heavily marked, old males almost pure white.
Legs and feet heavily feathered.
Compared with the american barn owl: Other white owls seen in most of North America are usually barn owls or downy young of other owls.

habitat.text: Open tundra; in winter prairies, fields, marshes, beaches, dunes and large airports.

behavior.text: Often hunts by day from a perch, watching for prey, then pursuing it in swift flight
Eats lemmings and voles where available, plus hares, rabbits, ground squirrels and birds
Nomadic; the number moving south each winter varies with prey populations
Usually silent; hoarse croak and shrill whistle on breeding grounds; males hoot to defend territory

resources.title: Pelagic cormorant
resources.description: Identify the pelagic cormorant (Urile pelagicus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pelagic cormorant (Urile pelagicus): Smallest Pacific-coast cormorant, 61-81 cm, with a small head and thin bill. Very glossy overall; dark red facial skin hard to see. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Pacific coast from the Bering Strait and Alaska south to Baja California, including British Columbia; northernmost breeders move south in winter.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe uses Urile pelagicus (genus split from Phalacrocorax after Kennedy & Spencer 2014); Canadian government pages still list Phalacrocorax pelagicus.
Alaska names a season; its federal basis is unresolved

rangeSummary.value: Pacific coast from the Bering Strait and Alaska south to Baja California, including British Columbia; northernmost breeders move south in winter.

identification.text: Smallest Pacific-coast cormorant, 61-81 cm, with a small head and thin bill.
Very glossy overall; dark red facial skin hard to see.
Breeding adults show white flank patches.
Immatures plain dark brown, best identified by shape.
Compared with the other pacific-coast cormorants: Larger with a bigger head and thicker bill.

habitat.text: Rocky coasts, bays and sounds, usually close to shore, near deep water at cliff bases.

behavior.text: Dives from the surface to at least 120 ft, taking fish near the bottom over rocky reefs
Forages singly; groups perch on rocks with wings held out to dry
Nests in colonies on narrow near-vertical cliff ledges; male flashes white flank patches in display
Groaning and hissing calls at colonies; shy and hard to approach

resources.title: Indian peafowl
resources.description: Identify the indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus): Male: iridescent blue neck and breast, golden back and sides, long train with eye-spots. Female: brown, grey and cream with no train. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to India and southeastern Asia. Small semi-domesticated populations are introduced and established in scattered North American localities and Hawaii.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the former name Common Peafowl was changed to Indian Peafowl (AOU 2012).

rangeSummary.value: Native to India and southeastern Asia. Small semi-domesticated populations are introduced and established in scattered North American localities and Hawaii.

identification.text: Male: iridescent blue neck and breast, golden back and sides, long train with eye-spots.
Female: brown, grey and cream with no train.
Juveniles light yellow to brown and resemble the female; males take about 3 years to grow the train.
Weighs 2.7-6 kg; both sexes have spurs (Animal Diversity Web).

habitat.text: Open forest, forest edge, second growth, scrub and cultivated land.

behavior.text: Solitary or in small groups outside breeding; roosts in trees, diurnal
Extremely loud harsh shrieking calls
Dust-bathes; eats insects, reptiles, seeds and grain
Polygynous; breeds about April-September

resources.title: Ringed turtle-dove
resources.description: Identify the ringed turtle-dove (Streptopelia risoria), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ringed turtle-dove (Streptopelia risoria): About 305 mm, warm creamy buff. Black semi-collar on the hind neck. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Sporadic introduced colonies near Los Angeles, in southern Florida and in Illinois.

taxonomicNotes.text: Animal Diversity Web treats it as a domesticated form of the African collared dove (S. roseogrisea); NatureServe lists S. roseogrisea, not S. risoria.
Domesticated form of the African collared-dove

rangeSummary.value: Sporadic introduced colonies near Los Angeles, in southern Florida and in Illinois.

identification.text: About 305 mm, warm creamy buff.
Black semi-collar on the hind neck.
Ruby-red eyes and purplish-red feet.
Slightly larger than the African collared dove with a shorter tail.
Compared with the eurasian collared-dove: Animal Diversity Web notes it resembles this species but the ringed turtle-dove is markedly tamer.

habitat.text: Domestic aviary birds; wild ancestor lives in African scrub, savanna and woodland.

behavior.text: Advertising call is 'koo, krroo'; also a high-pitched excitement call
Displays with bowing and wing-clapping display flights
Eats grains and seeds without husking

content.plainText: Confirm a green pheasant before you act. Compared with the ring-necked pheasant: Considered by some authorities the same species; Hawaii records also mention a melanistic 'mutant' or blue form of ring-necked pheasant that can resemble green pheasant.
Confirm a japanese quail before you act. Compared with the common quail: Very similar; the two are sympatric in Mongolia without interbreeding (ADW, NatureServe).
Confirm a rock partridge before you act. Compared with the chukar: Very similar; rock partridge is greyer on the back with a white foreneck instead of yellowish.
Confirm a red-legged partridge before you act. Compared with the rock partridge: Sharply defined black gorget without streaking below it; greyer back.
Confirm a spotted dove before you act. Compared with the mourning dove: Spotted dove is bulkier with a rounder tail, has no black wing spots and shows the white-spotted black neck collar.

Confirm a zebra dove before you act. Compared with the peaceful dove: Australian/New Guinea species that some authors have treated as part of the same species; not found in North America (NatureServe, Bishop Museum).
Confirm a white-tipped dove before you act. Compared with the mourning dove: White-tipped is much rounder-bodied and shorter-tailed with pale eyes, and lacks the black ear spot and black wing spots.
Confirm a rock pigeon before you act. Compared with the band-tailed pigeon: Wild native pigeon that some feral Rock Pigeon colour forms can suggest; Audubon gives no further separating marks.
Confirm a mottled duck before you act. Compared with the mallard (female): Mottled Duck is darker and its wing patch lacks Mallard's broad white borders.
Confirm a mexican duck before you act. Compared with the mallard (female): Mexican Duck is somewhat darker, especially on the tail and undertail, with narrower white wing-patch borders.

Confirm a fulvous whistling-duck before you act. Compared with the black-bellied whistling-duck (young): Audubon says to compare young Black-bellied with Fulvous; Fulvous is uniformly butterscotch with a gray bill and white flank stripes.
Confirm a eurasian wigeon before you act. Compared with the american wigeon: Female is very much alike; Eurasian may have a browner head. Hybrids are rare and intermediate.

Confirm a emperor goose before you act. Compared with the snow goose (blue morph): Emperor Goose has a black foreneck and chin and a scaly body pattern; the blue morph has a gray body and white head without them.

Confirm a double-crested cormorant before you act. Compared with the great cormorant: Larger and bulkier with a broad white band across the throat, dull yellow (not orange) throat pouch and, when breeding, white flank patches.
Confirm a great cormorant before you act. Compared with the double-crested cormorant: Smaller; orange throat pouch and no broad white throat band or white flank patches.
Confirm a thick-billed murre before you act. Compared with the common murre: Slightly thinner bill without the white gape mark; less black on the face in winter; avoids pack-ice areas.
Confirm a common murre before you act. Compared with the thick-billed murre: Slightly thicker bill with a white mark at the gape, blacker back, and often more black on the face in winter.
Confirm a common raven before you act. Compared with the chihuahuan raven: Audubon says to compare it in the Southwest but gives no separating marks.
Confirm a black-billed magpie before you act. Compared with the yellow-billed magpie: Found in California; the Black-billed has a black bill (Audubon says to see Yellow-billed there).
Confirm a brewer's blackbird before you act. Compared with the rusty blackbird: Rusty is less glossy with a thinner bill, yellow eyes and, in fall, rusty feather edges.
Confirm a rusty blackbird before you act. Compared with the brewer's blackbird: Brewer's male is glossier with a thicker bill; ranges mainly west of Rusty's range.
Confirm a bronzed cowbird before you act. Compared with the brown-headed cowbird: Bronzed is larger with a longer bill, shorter tail, red eye and neck ruff.
Confirm a shiny cowbird before you act. Compared with the brown-headed cowbird: Similar in size and shape; the male Shiny is entirely black with purple gloss, and females are not safely separated.
Confirm a common grackle before you act. Compared with the great-tailed grackle: Larger with a much longer tail and more evenly coloured male.
Confirm a great-tailed grackle before you act. Compared with the common grackle: Smaller with a shorter tail and less evenly coloured male.
